newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine rights groups hail Galtieri arrest warrant.
newsitem.headline: Argentine rights groups hail Galtieri arrest warrant.

text.p: Argentine human rights groups reacted with joy on Tuesday to news that Spain had issued an international arrest warrant for former Argentine military president Leopoldo Galtieri.

"We think it's fantastic that the world is starting to prosecute these killers," the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo leader Hebe de Bonafini told Reuters. "What we would like is for all these criminals to be brought to justice."

The Mothers of Plaza de Mayo are relatives of some of the up to 30,000 people abducted and killed by the military during their 1976-83 regime. In their famed white headscarves, they have marched in Buenos Aires' Plaza de Mayo for two decades to demand information about the fate of their loved ones.
Galtieri, 70, led Argentina's former military junta from 1980 to 1982, and ordered the invasion of the Falkland Islands that led to a disastrous 10-week war with Britain.

There was a jubilant reaction to news of the arrest warrant from the Peace and Justice Service (SERPAJ) led by Adolfo Perez Esquivel, who won the Nobel Peace Prize for his campaign against the "Dirty War".

SERPAJ called the decision by Spanish High Court Judge Baltasar Garzon a boost for "the fight against impunity" and said, "Until now there has been no way of making international law effective. This will allow justice to be done for Spain and Argentina."

Garzon, who is investigating the disappearance of 300 Spanish nationals in the "Dirty War" on leftists, ordered Galtieri's arrest if he leaves Argentina for allegedly ordering the death of Spanish citizen Victor Labrador and his two sons in 1976.

It is Garzon's first arrest warrant in a year-long probe. But Galtieri is unlikely to face trial in Spain. Argentina says it cannot extradite anyone for Dirty War trials as they were tried in Argentina after democracy returned in 1983.

France has an arrest warrant out for former Argentine Navy Capt. Alfredo Astiz, known as the "Blond Angel", and has sentenced him in absentia to life in prison for the murder of two French nuns in the first years of the military regime.
French President Jacques Chirac urged on a recent visit to Argentina that Astiz be tried in France, but Justice Minister Elias Jassan insists that the Dirty War crimes are "a closed case."
Like Astiz and all Dirty War criminals, Galtieri was freed under an amnesty ordered by President Carlos Menem in 1989.
